edges.effect_quant: A meta-analysis of 17 studies including 3230 participants found only 2 studies in which vegans had vitamin B12 and homocysteine concentrations comparable with omnivores, while a Lebanese cross-sectional study of 483 adults found 43.1% overall B12 deficiency and greater susceptibility among vegans and vegetarians.
edges.population: vegetarians and vegans across childhood and adulthood
edges.mechanism: Vitamin B12 is supplied almost entirely by animal-derived foods, so plant-only or animal-restricted diets can gradually exhaust hepatic B12 stores unless fortified foods or supplements are used. As stores fall, methylmalonic acid and homocysteine can rise before overt hematologic or neurologic complications emerge.
edges.summary: Vegetarian and especially vegan eating patterns are consistently linked to lower vitamin B12 status and higher deficiency risk when supplementation is absent or inconsistent. The signal is strong enough to treat B12 coverage as a routine requirement of plant-based diets rather than an optional optimization.
edges.caveats: This is not an inevitable consequence of every vegetarian diet, because regular supplementation or well-fortified foods can largely prevent deficiency. Risk varies by diet strictness, duration of adherence, pregnancy status, and how deficiency is defined biochemically.
